desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

The list is sorted in non-decreasing order of absolute value: |nums[0]| ≤ |nums[1]| ≤ .... Values with equal absolute value may appear in any order (for example 3, -3, 3). Return the list sorted in ordinary non-decreasing order of the values themselves.

For example [0,1,-2,3,-4] becomes [-4,-2,0,1,3]. A general O(n log n) sort works, but the existing order lets you finish in O(n) time by relinking nodes.
hints: Look at the negative values only. In which order do they appear compared to the order they must have in the answer?
The negatives appear with growing magnitude, e.g. -1, -2, -4, but the sorted answer needs -4, -2, -1: they are in exactly the reverse order. The non-negative values are already in the right order.

Walk the list; whenever a node has a negative value, unlink it and put it in front of the current head. Moving each negative to the front reverses the negatives while the non-negatives keep their relative order.
editorial: Split the list mentally into two subsequences. The non-negative values appear in increasing order because their absolute value equals their value. The negative values appear with increasing magnitude, which means decreasing value, so they are in exactly the reverse of the order they need.

So one pass is enough: keep a prev pointer, and for each node whose value is negative unlink it and insert it before the current head (it becomes the new head). Moving every negative to the front reverses their order and leaves the non-negatives in place. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
Equal absolute values need no special care: a run like 3, -3, 3 turns into -3, 3, 3 because the negative is pulled to the front while the others keep their order.
